---
title: "Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it"
subtitle: "A one-time cleanup that gets a real research folder into shape for an agent."
---

If you're like most economists, your active research folders look something
like this:

```
~/Dropbox/wage-paper/
├── paper.tex
├── paper_v2.tex
├── paper_FINAL.tex
├── paper_FINAL_resubmit.tex
├── clean.do
├── clean_OLD.do
├── analysis_v3_rebuttal.do
├── estimate.jl
├── estimate_test.jl
├── make_figures.R
├── make_figures_v2.R
├── data.dta
├── data_clean.dta
├── data_v3_no_outliers.dta
├── results.csv
├── results_old.csv
├── tables/
├── tables_old/
├── tables_referee2/
├── notes.txt
└── (50 more files)
```

There is no README. The "live" version of `paper.tex` is in your head, not
on disk. The Stata cleaning scripts call into Julia for estimation and R
for figures, but nothing documents the order. Three of the `.do` files
run; one runs but produces the wrong table; the other two break. The
Julia files in `estimate_test.jl` are an old structural model; the live
one is in `estimate.jl`. Two of the `.dta` files are inputs to something;
the rest are dead. Half the scripts have hardcoded paths to your
coauthor's Dropbox folder.

::: {.callout-note}
**The example project on this page is intentionally multi-language**
(Stata for cleaning, Julia for estimation, R for figures, LaTeX for the
paper) because that's how a lot of empirical and structural work
actually looks. Every prompt and snippet on this page works the same
way whether your project is one language or four — just adjust the
file extensions and the runner commands. If you're a one-language
shop, the multi-language bits will read as harmless extras.
:::

This is fine for a human who wrote it. It is bad for Claude Code, which
will read everything, get confused about which version is canonical, and
either ask you a lot of questions or — worse — confidently edit the
wrong file.

**This page walks you through a one-time reorganization** that gets the
project into shape for agentic work. It is itself a perfect first project
for Claude Code, because the agent can do most of the work and the worst
case is recoverable.

::: {.callout-warning}
**The single most important rule on this page: never reorganize the live
project.** Always work on a copy. The first step below explains how.
:::

## What "ready for Claude Code" actually means

You are aiming for a project where:

- A stranger (or a future-you, or an RA, or Claude Code) can open the
  folder and figure out what's going on within five minutes.
- There is a single **master script** that runs every step from raw data
  to final tables and the compiled paper.
- **Live code** is clearly distinguished from old/exploratory code. The
  archive is preserved, not deleted.
- Every dependency between files is explicit (no hidden assumptions about
  what was last run by hand in Stata's window).
- A `CLAUDE.md` file at the root tells Claude what's specific to your
  project: language version, conventions, what's off-limits, where the
  data is, what the master script is.
- A `README.md` tells a human reader the same things.
- `.gitignore` keeps derived files and OS junk out of git.
- Git is initialized so any change is recoverable.

A reasonable target structure (adjust to taste):

```
project-name/
├── README.md
├── CLAUDE.md
├── .gitignore
├── make-all.sh           (top-level orchestrator; calls each language in order)
├── data/
│   ├── raw/              (read-only; never modified by code)
│   └── derived/          (built from raw/ by code/)
├── code/
│   ├── 01-clean.do          (Stata: prep raw data)
│   ├── 02-estimate.jl       (Julia: structural estimation)
│   ├── 03-counterfactuals.jl (Julia: simulate)
│   └── 04-figures.R         (R: ggplot tables and figures)
├── output/
│   ├── tables/
│   └── figures/
├── paper/
│   ├── paper.tex
│   ├── references.bib
│   └── (figures, tables, etc.)
├── docs/                 (data dictionaries, notes, source docs)
└── archive/              (everything you didn't delete but isn't live)
```

The single `code/` folder mixes Stata, Julia, and R because that's how
the work flows — the numeric prefixes (`01-`, `02-`, …) make the order
obvious regardless of language. Some people prefer `code/stata/`,
`code/julia/`, `code/r/` subfolders instead; either works as long as
the orchestrator at the top knows the order.

This is a default, not a religion. AEA, TIER, BITSS, and the Reardon
protocol all propose variations — pick one and stick to it.

## The walkthrough

Each step has the prompt you'd give Claude Code (in the integrated
terminal of [VS Code](vscode.qmd) or in a bare terminal — your choice).
Read every diff — the exact lines each change touched — before approving.

### Step 1 — Copy the project to a working directory

Do this in the terminal yourself, not through Claude. It is one command
and it is the safety net for everything that follows.

```bash
cp -R ~/Dropbox/wage-paper ~/Desktop/wage-paper-cleanup
```

Or, on a Mac, use Finder: select the folder, `Cmd-D` to duplicate,
move the duplicate somewhere outside Dropbox.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Already git-fluent and the original project is already in git? Use a
worktree instead of `cp -R`.**

```bash
cd ~/projects/wage-paper            # the original, already in git
git worktree add ../wage-paper-cleanup -b reorganize-2026
cd ../wage-paper-cleanup            # work here for the rest of this page
```

This replaces both Step 1 (copy) *and* Step 2 (`git init` + first
commit). The worktree is a fresh working directory on its own branch,
with the current `main` commit as the implicit baseline. You can skip
ahead to Step 3.

A worktree gives you everything `cp -R` does, plus several real wins
specific to a multi-step reorganization:

- **The reorganization is a reviewable change set.** At the end,
  `git diff main..reorganize-2026` shows the entire transformation as
  one diff you (and a coauthor, and Claude) can read.
- **Each step is its own commit on the branch.** `git log
  reorganize-2026` is your audit trail. If a verification run fails
  three days from now, `git bisect` finds the exact commit that broke
  the result.
- **History stays connected to the original.** Mid-reorganization, if
  a referee asks something about the published structure, `cd
  ~/projects/wage-paper` and the original is right there, untouched
  and on `main`. With `cp -R` you'd have two disconnected copies and
  no easy way to compare.
- **Coauthor review before you commit to it.** Push the branch; your
  coauthor reviews `reorganize-2026` as a pull request and either
  approves the new structure or flags issues *before* you merge into
  `main`. A `cp -R` copy is invisible to them until you finish.
- **One-command cleanup if you abandon halfway:** `git worktree remove
  ../wage-paper-cleanup && git branch -D reorganize-2026`. Compared to
  `rm -rf` of a `cp -R` copy, this is the same outcome but with a
  paper trail in `git reflog` if you change your mind tomorrow.
- **The `.gitignore` you'll write in Step 12 stays applied across
  reorganization steps automatically.** No risk of accidentally
  committing build artifacts or derived data because the rules are
  inherited from the branch.

If you're new to Git — or the original project isn't yet in git — the
`cp -R` path below is the recommended default.
The full explanation of worktrees, with more use cases and pitfalls,
is in the [Worktrees section of the Git page](git.qmd#worktrees-when-one-working-directory-isnt-enough).
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Move the copy outside any cloud-synced folder** (Dropbox, OneDrive,
iCloud Drive). Reorganization will rename and move many files; you don't
want every intermediate state syncing across your devices and your
coauthors' machines. Once you're done and verified, you can move the
finished version back.

If your project contains **IRB-protected, restricted-access, or
otherwise confidential data**, stop and read [Confidential
data](../pitfalls/confidential-data.qmd) before doing anything else.
At minimum, make sure the data subfolder is not pulled into the working
copy unless you've confirmed it's safe to send to a cloud LLM provider
in subsequent steps.
:::

Verify the copy:

```bash
du -sh ~/Dropbox/wage-paper ~/Desktop/wage-paper-cleanup
```

Sizes should match within a few KB. Now `cd` into the copy and from
this point on, work only there.

```bash
cd ~/Desktop/wage-paper-cleanup
```

### Step 2 — Initialize git in the copy

Even if you never push to GitHub, local git is the recoverable history
that makes the rest of this walkthrough safe. From inside the copy:

```bash
git init -b main
git add -A
git commit -m "Baseline before reorganization"
```

Now any change Claude makes is undoable with `git checkout .` or
`git reset --hard HEAD`. This is the foundation of the
"[robust system with fail-safes](../principles.qmd)" principle.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Never used Git?** Read the [Git page](git.qmd) before this step. The
five-minute version: Git takes
snapshots of your project; every snapshot is permanent locally; you
can always go back. Without Git, you have no fail-safe under what
follows; with Git, every step on this page is one keystroke away from
undoable.
:::

### Step 3 — Open Claude Code and take inventory

Start Claude in the copy:

```bash
claude
```

First prompt — purely read-only. You're asking for a map, not an action:

> *"Read the entire project. Don't modify anything. Produce a Markdown
> inventory with: (a) every top-level file and directory, (b) for each
> code file, a one-line description of what it appears to do, (c) for
> each data file, its size and a guess at whether it looks like raw
> input or derived output, (d) for each .tex file, whether it appears
> to be a paper draft, an old version, an appendix, slides, or
> something else. End with a section called 'Open questions' — things
> you'd need me to confirm before reorganizing."*

You will get back a 2-4 page document. Read it carefully. This is where
you discover that `analysis_v3_rebuttal.do` is actually the live one and
`analysis.do` is from two years ago — exactly the kind of thing a clean
reorganization needs to get right.

### Step 4 — Identify the live code path

Now narrow the inventory to what currently matters:

> *"Based on the inventory, identify the **live code path** — the
> minimal set of scripts and data files needed to reproduce the current
> version of `paper.tex` (or whichever .tex file I confirm is live).
> Trace dependencies: which scripts read which data files, which
> scripts produce which intermediate files, which scripts produce the
> tables and figures cited in the paper. Output as a Markdown list.
> Don't move or delete anything yet."*

If Claude is unsure which `.tex` is the live paper, it will ask. Tell it.

What you get is a dependency map. Everything *not* on it is a candidate
for archiving in step 6.

::: {.callout-warning}
**This is the step where Claude can hallucinate dependencies.** Spot-check
a few of its claims. Open a script Claude says produces Table 3; confirm
it does. Open a `.dta` Claude says is unused; grep for its name across
the project to make sure nothing references it. The cost of a
hallucinated "this file is dead" is real — you might archive a file that
something obscure actually needs.
:::

### Step 5 — Confirm and adjust the live path manually

This step is for you, not Claude. Read the dependency map. Add anything
Claude missed. Remove anything you know is actually dead. The output of
this step is your confirmed list of "what stays in the live path."

A useful question to ask yourself for ambiguous files: **"if this file
went missing tomorrow, would I notice?"** If no, archive. If yes, live.

### Step 6 — Move exploration to `archive/`, don't delete

Now the first real edit. Tell Claude:

> *"Create an `archive/` directory. Move every file and folder NOT on
> the confirmed live-path list into `archive/`, preserving relative
> structure inside `archive/` so I can find things later. Use `git mv`
> so the moves are tracked. Don't delete anything. Show me the plan
> before executing."*

Use [plan mode](plan-mode-and-todo.qmd) for this — `Shift+Tab` until you
see "plan mode" before you send the prompt. You want to read the full
move list before any file is touched.

When the moves are done, commit:

```bash
git add -A
git commit -m "Archive non-live files"
```

::: {.callout-tip}
**Why archive instead of delete?** You will be wrong about what's dead
roughly 10% of the time. A coauthor will ask "what happened to the
robustness check that used `wage_no_outliers.dta`?" and the answer
"in `archive/data/wage_no_outliers.dta`" is much better than "I deleted
it last Tuesday."
:::

### Step 7 — Standardize the folder structure

Propose first, move second:

> *"I want to reorganize the live files into this structure:
> [paste the target structure from earlier on this page, edited for
> your project]. Propose how to map every current live file into the
> target structure. Don't move anything yet. Flag any files where you're
> not sure where they belong, and any files in the target structure
> that don't exist yet (e.g., I have no `master.do` — that's fine,
> we'll create it later)."*

Read the proposed mapping. Adjust anything that's wrong. Then:

> *"Execute the mapping. Use `git mv`. Do not modify file contents —
> only move and rename. After every move, update path references in the
> remaining live files so the project still resolves. Cover each
> language's idioms:
> Stata (`include`, `do`, `use ... , clear`, `save`, `import delimited`),
> R (`source()`, `here::here()`, `readr::read_*()`, `setwd()`,
> `ggsave()`),
> Julia (`include()`, `using`, `CSV.read`, `joinpath()`, `Pkg.activate`),
> Python (`import`, `from ... import`, `pathlib.Path`, `pd.read_*`,
> `open()`),
> LaTeX (`\input{}`, `\includegraphics{}`, `\addbibresource{}`),
> Matlab (`addpath`, `cd`, `load`, `readtable`).
> Show me each path-fix diff before applying."*

Plan mode again. Approve diffs one at a time. Commit when done:

```bash
git commit -am "Reorganize live files into standard structure"
```

### Step 8 — Find and fix hardcoded paths

> *"Search the entire project (excluding `archive/`) for hardcoded
> absolute paths — anything starting with `/Users/`, `/home/`,
> `C:\\`, `~/Dropbox`, or that references a specific user's folder.
> List every occurrence with file and line number. Don't change
> anything yet."*

You'll get a list. For each hardcoded path, decide:

- **Convert to relative.** Best default. `/Users/me/Dropbox/wage-paper/data/raw.dta`
  becomes `data/raw/raw.dta`.
- **Move to a config block.** If the path points outside the project
  (a shared dataset on a research drive, say), put it in a small
  `config.do` (or `config.R`, etc.) at the project root and `include`
  it from each script. One place to change paths when machines change.
- **Document but leave alone.** If the path is to a restricted-access
  data folder that genuinely lives elsewhere, document the requirement
  in the README and leave the path. Hardcoding is a feature here.

Then ask Claude to apply the conversion you decided:

> *"Convert paths in [list of files] from absolute to relative,
> assuming the project root is the working directory. Show diffs."*

Commit when done.

### Step 9 — Draft `CLAUDE.md`

`CLAUDE.md` is read by Claude at the start of every session in this
project. See [Memory, CLAUDE.md, skills](../workflow/memory-and-claude-md.qmd)
for the full picture; for now:

> *"Write a `CLAUDE.md` at the project root with:
> (1) one-paragraph description of what the project is and its current
> status,
> (2) the **full stack** — for every language used in `code/`, the
> version (Stata 18, R 4.4, Julia 1.11, Python 3.12, …) and the key
> packages, plus the LaTeX distribution and any Stata/R packages that
> aren't on the default path,
> (3) folder conventions in this project (`data/raw/` is read-only;
> `output/` is built; etc.),
> (4) the orchestrator (`make-all.sh` or `Makefile`) and how to run it,
> including the order in which the languages are invoked and any
> language-specific gotchas (e.g., 'the Stata binary on this machine is
> `stata-mp`'),
> (5) what to never do (don't modify `data/raw/`, don't commit
> `data/derived/`, don't change `paper/paper.tex` without asking, etc.),
> (6) anything else a new collaborator would need.
> Read what's already in the project to fill in real values; ask me
> where you're unsure."*

Read what Claude produces. Edit it freely — this is *your* document.
Commit.

### Step 10 — Draft `README.md`

`README.md` is the human-facing version of `CLAUDE.md`, plus more
context. Same principle: have Claude draft, you edit.

> *"Write a `README.md` at the project root following the AEA data and
> code availability standards: (1) project description and citation,
> (2) data availability and provenance — for each dataset in `data/raw/`,
> where it came from, whether it's public or restricted, how to obtain
> it if restricted, (3) computational requirements — software, packages,
> expected runtime, (4) instructions to reproduce — exactly what
> command(s) someone runs from a clean clone, (5) a mapping from each
> table and figure in `paper/paper.tex` to the script and output file
> that produces it, (6) license. Use what's already in CLAUDE.md and
> the code; ask me where you're unsure."*

::: {.callout-warning}
**Read this draft critically.** Claude can write a plausible-looking
README that overstates how complete the project is. The data-availability
section in particular: if your raw data came from a confidential source,
say so explicitly and don't let Claude paper over it.
:::

Edit, commit.

### Step 11 — Build a master script (the orchestrator)

If your project mixes languages — Stata cleaning, then Julia estimation,
then R figures, then a LaTeX compile — no single language's script can
sit at the top. You want a **language-agnostic orchestrator** at the
project root that calls each runner in order. A small shell script is
the simplest answer; a `Makefile` is the upgrade path.

The prompt:

> *"Write a `make-all.sh` shell script at the project root that runs
> the full pipeline in order: invoke each language's runner for the
> scripts in `code/` (Stata for `.do`, Julia for `.jl`, R for `.R`,
> Python for `.py` if any), then compile `paper/paper.tex`. Use
> `set -euo pipefail` so the script halts on the first error. `cd` to
> the project root at the top so it works from anywhere. Print a
> one-line progress message before each step and a one-line success
> message at the end. Use relative paths."*

You'll get something like:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"   # always run from project root

echo "[1/4] Cleaning data (Stata)..."
stata-mp -b do code/01-clean.do

echo "[2/4] Estimating model (Julia)..."
julia --project code/02-estimate.jl

echo "[3/4] Producing figures and tables (R)..."
Rscript code/04-figures.R

echo "[4/4] Compiling paper..."
( cd paper && latexmk -pdf paper.tex )

echo "Done. Outputs in output/, paper in paper/paper.pdf."
```

Make it executable once: `chmod +x make-all.sh`. From then on, one
command rebuilds the whole project: `./make-all.sh`.

::: {.callout-note}
**Single-language project?** If everything is Stata, a `master.do` at
the root that `do`s each script is fine. If everything is R,
`master.R` calling `source()` on each script works. The orchestrator
matters most when you cross language boundaries; below that, use what
your language gives you.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**A `Makefile` is the upgrade.** Once your pipeline is stable and slow,
a Makefile pays for itself: it re-runs only what's downstream of the
file you changed. For most econ projects you don't need it on day
one — but if a single rebuild starts taking 20+ minutes, that's the
signal to convert your `make-all.sh` into a Makefile with proper
`target: prerequisite` rules.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Stata's batch flag varies by platform and version.** On Mac/Linux the
typical invocation is `stata-mp -b do script.do`; on Windows it's
`StataMP.exe /e do script.do`. If your group uses Stata-SE or
Stata-IC, the binary names differ (`stata-se`, `stata`). Tell Claude
which binary you have in `CLAUDE.md` so it gets it right the first time.
:::

### Step 12 — Add `.gitignore`

> *"Write a `.gitignore` for this project. Exclude:
> (a) **LaTeX build artifacts**: `*.aux`, `*.log`, `*.out`, `*.toc`,
> `*.blg`, `*.bbl`, `*.synctex.gz`, `*.fls`, `*.fdb_latexmk`;
> (b) **Stata**: `*.smcl` log files (large; usually you only want the
> `.log` ASCII version); also Stata's per-user temp files;
> (c) **R**: `.Rhistory`, `.Rproj.user/`, `.Rdata`, `.RData`;
> (d) **Julia**: `*.cov`. Decide whether to commit `Manifest.toml`:
> commit it if you want bit-exact reproducibility (recommended for
> replication packages); leave it ignored if you want package-version
> flexibility while you're still developing;
> (e) **Python**: `__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, `.ipynb_checkpoints/`,
> `.venv/`;
> (f) **Matlab**: `*.asv` (autosaves), `*.mexmaci64`, `*.mexmaca64`,
> `*.mexa64`, `*.mexw64` (compiled MEX files);
> (g) **OS junk**: `.DS_Store` (macOS), `Thumbs.db` (Windows);
> (h) **Derived data**: `data/derived/**`;
> (i) **Editor cruft**: `.vscode/` (unless you want to commit shared
> settings), `.idea/`.
> Show me the file before creating it."*

After it's in place, clean up anything that's already tracked but should
be ignored:

```bash
git rm -r --cached data/derived
git commit -m "Stop tracking derived data"
```

::: {.callout-tip}
**One subtle Julia decision.** `Project.toml` should always be committed
— it lists which packages your code uses. `Manifest.toml` is the
exact-version lockfile. For an active research project, ignoring
`Manifest.toml` is fine (and keeps merge conflicts down with coauthors).
For a replication package, commit it — readers should get the exact
package versions you used.
:::

### Step 13 — Run end-to-end and verify

The whole point of the orchestrator and the clean structure is that you
can do this:

```bash
# In the terminal, from the project root:
./make-all.sh        # or `make all` if you went the Makefile route
```

Or have Claude do it:

> *"Run `./make-all.sh` from a fresh state. If any step errors, stop
> and tell me what happened — don't try to auto-fix. After it succeeds,
> list every file produced under `output/` and `paper/`, confirm the
> paper PDF compiled without unresolved references or missing-citation
> warnings, and report the total wall-clock runtime."*

If the master script doesn't reproduce something that's in your paper,
that's a real finding — either the live code path is wrong (re-do
step 4) or there's an undocumented manual step somewhere (document it
in the README).

When everything runs end-to-end, commit:

```bash
git commit -am "Reorganization complete; master script reproduces all results"
```

### Step 14 — Compare against the original

You worked in a copy. Before throwing away the original, do one final
diff:

> *"List every table and figure file in the original project at
> `~/Dropbox/wage-paper/` (read-only — don't modify anything there).
> For each, find the corresponding file in this reorganized project
> and compare. Flag any tables or figures that exist in the original
> but not here (might be missing live code), or that exist here but
> have different content (might be a numerical regression)."*

Investigate any flags. When the diff is clean, the reorganized version
is your new live project. Move it back to its permanent home (out of
`~/Desktop/`), update any external references, and you are done.

## Things to be careful about

- **Work in a copy, never on top of the original.** The whole approach
  rests on this.
- **Archive, don't delete.** The cost of an over-aggressive archive is
  fishing a file out of `archive/`; the cost of an over-aggressive delete
  is rebuilding work from memory.
- **Some files look unused but aren't.** A `.dta` with no matching `use`
  might be loaded inside an `include`d script, called from a Matlab
  routine, or read by a coauthor's pipeline. Spot-check before archiving.
- **Talk to coauthors before reorganizing a shared project.** A unilateral
  reorganization makes you the only person who can find anything for a
  month. Do it on a branch, share the new structure, then merge.
- **`git mv` preserves history but resets filesystem `mtime`.** If
  anything you use depends on file timestamps, note it.
- **Confidential data is its own decision.** If `data/raw/` is
  restricted-access, was Claude reading it during the inventory step? If
  that's not OK, move or symlink the data out *before* starting Claude.
  See [Confidential data](../pitfalls/confidential-data.qmd).

## When *not* to reorganize

- **Right before a deadline** — the risk of silently breaking something
  outweighs the benefit.
- **For a project you're about to abandon** — just archive the whole
  folder.
- **Without a copy** — see above.
- **On someone else's published replication package** — that's a
  different workflow; see the
  [replication-package audit](../examples/replication-package.qmd).

A typical mid-sized project (one paper, 20–40 files, a few hundred MB)
takes half a day to a full day the first time, most of it your own
reading and judgment rather than waiting on Claude. It goes faster once
the steps are familiar.
